sectors.title: Technology
sectors.summary: Software, product, design, data. There is far more of this work in Ireland than you'd expect, and plenty of it is in Irish companies nobody outside the industry has heard of. A computer science degree is the usual way in. It is not the only one. Apprenticeships exist here and hardly anyone advertises them, and after a first job almost nobody asks where you studied.

sectors.title: Healthcare
sectors.summary: Medicine, nursing, physiotherapy, pharmacy, occupational therapy, and a long list of jobs that never come up in careers talks. Some of the steadiest work in the country. The ways in vary more than students expect. Straight from the Leaving Cert for some. A conversion course ten years later for others.

sectors.title: Law
sectors.summary: Solicitor, barrister, legal executive, or in-house at a company. The usual path is a law degree and then professional exams. Graduate entry is normal too, and the legal executive route needs no degree at all. Firms run from big Dublin practices to one-solicitor offices, and the work is nothing alike.

sectors.title: Finance
sectors.summary: Banking, accountancy, insurance, fintech, and the public sector. Several of the accounting qualifications can be earned while you are employed and paid. Students are rarely told that, and it changes the maths on the whole thing.

sectors.title: Trades
sectors.summary: Some of the most in-demand work in the country and the worst explained. You get in through a SOLAS apprenticeship: paid from year one, no college fees, qualified in about four years. Long-term security, the option of working for yourself, and a route on into contracting and running sites. If a student is being quietly written off, this is usually the conversation nobody has had with them.

sectors.title: Media & communications
sectors.summary: Journalism, broadcasting, PR, marketing, content. An old tradition in the first two and a fast-moving industry in the rest. There are courses. There is also the route of building a body of work until somebody notices, which is harder than it sounds and more common than it used to be.

sectors.title: Education
sectors.summary: Teaching, special education, youth work, further education, educational psychology. Primary teaching has its own degree. Secondary is usually a subject degree and then a masters. Youth and community work has ways in that need no traditional degree, and they are rarely mentioned.

sectors.title: Engineering
sectors.summary: Civil, mechanical, electrical, biomedical, manufacturing. Ireland does a lot of medical devices and pharmaceutical manufacturing, which is invisible to students unless someone points at the building. Degree or higher apprenticeship. Technician routes offer a paid way in without four years up front.

sectors.title: Public sector
sectors.summary: The civil service, local authorities, An Garda Síochána, the Defence Forces, the state agencies. A lot of it is filled by open competition rather than by degree requirement. The Leaving Cert is enough for a number of entry grades, with a clear way up afterwards. Almost nobody explains this to sixth years.

sectors.title: Other sectors
sectors.summary: Mentors whose work does not sit neatly above. Agriculture, hospitality, the arts, sport, logistics, charities.
